rationale: This mixed-methods case study of four Ethiopian cities (Addis Ababa, Adama, Mekelle, and Dire Dawa) combines key informant interviews and field observations with field hydraulic/chlorine measurements, secondary utility records, demand projections, and ArcGIS/WaterGEMS network simulations. While much of the paper evaluates engineering, hydraulic, and environmental challenges, its empirical institutional and governance analysis (Sections 4.1.8 and 4.2.5) centers on institutional_structure_coordination—specifically incomplete decentralization, local government dependence on regional states, split mandates where local water enterprises supply water while regional water bureaus control project structure and financing, over-centralization, and weak coordination across federal, state, and local water institutions (with secondary discussion of the corporatized 'Enterprise model'/private sector participation and lack of citizen participation). The central access outcomes analyzed are effective_access dimensions: intermittent (non-24/7) supply, volumetric supply-demand deficits, low-pressure nodal delivery shortfalls, residual chlorine and source water quality, and long-term functional sustainability. Confidence is medium because legal/governance rules form one qualitative sub-component of a predominantly engineering-focused assessment.
